title: Decision Trees & Ensembles
why: Gradient-boosted trees still win most tabular-data problems in industry, and trees are a favorite interview topic.
explain: A decision tree asks a sequence of yes/no questions about features. At each node it picks the split that most reduces impurity, using Gini = 1 - sum(p^2) or entropy = -sum(p log p), then recurses until a stopping rule (maximum depth, minimum samples) is reached. Trees handle mixed feature types and need little preprocessing, but a single deep tree overfits badly.

Ensembles fix that. Bagging and random forests train many trees on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets and average their votes, which reduces variance. Boosting (gradient boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM) builds trees one after another, each correcting the previous errors, which reduces bias.

Feature importance comes from how much each feature reduces impurity, or from permutation importance, which is less biased. Trees are piecewise constant, so they cannot extrapolate beyond the range seen in training.
key_points: Greedy split search: try thresholds, keep the best impurity decrease
Depth and minimum-leaf size control overfitting
Random forest = bagging + random feature subsets (variance reduction)
Boosting fits residual errors sequentially (bias reduction)
Permutation importance on held-out data is more trustworthy than impurity importance
pitfalls: Impurity importance favors high-cardinality features such as IDs
Trees cannot extrapolate beyond the training range

leetcode.why: Recursive depth is the same recursion you use to limit tree growth.
Building a tree from traversals practices constructing nodes recursively from partitioned data.
Validating a BST with value ranges mirrors how split thresholds bound each child.
Partitioning an array around a pivot is exactly what a split does to samples.
Aggregating gains from subtrees in post-order is the pattern behind pruning and boosting gain calculations.

industry.q: Why does a random forest generalize better than one deep decision tree?
key_points: Single deep trees have high variance
Bootstrap samples and random feature subsets decorrelate the trees
Out-of-bag samples give a free validation estimate

industry.q: Random forest or gradient boosting: when do you choose each?
key_points: Forest: robust defaults, parallel, hard to overfit badly
Boosting: usually higher accuracy but needs tuning and early stopping
Consider training time and interpretability needs

industry.q: Impurity-based feature importance ranks a customer ID column highly. Why, and what do you do?
key_points: High-cardinality features offer many split points, which biases importance
Use permutation importance on validation data
